newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK invites 60 Taiwanese, Beijing-Taipeh talks seen.
newsitem.headline: HK invites 60 Taiwanese, Beijing-Taipeh talks seen.

text.p: Hong Kong has invited officials from China's arch-rival Taiwan to celebrate the territory's handover to Beijing in a move that will make the seating plan trickier than a giant wedding banquet.
Diplomats predict representatives from Beijing and Taipeh will hold talks on the sidelines of the gala - despite strained ties and parallel military exercises later this month.
Stephen Lam, the Hong Kong government's chief coordinator of handover ceremonies, said 60 Taiwan officials had been invited but he gave no names or details.
"Basically, we have issued over 60 invitations to people from Taiwan, they are being invited in their personal capacities," Lam told reporters.
"As for seating arrangements...if you have done wedding banquets for two or three hundred people, you know how difficult it is, and now we are trying to do one for 4,000 people."
Britain, China and the Hong Kong government have invited over 4,000 people to an end-of-empire gala banquet and handover ceremony straddling midnight June 30 and the morning of July 1.
At the stroke of midnight, China will regain sovereignty over Hong Kong, ending 156 years of colonial rule which began with imperial China's humiliating defeat in the Opium Wars.
Britain's royal heir Prince Charles will hand back the territory to China's President Jiang Zemin.

China's late leader Deng Xiaoping devised a "one country two systems" policy for Hong Kong to keep its capitalist way of life for a further 50 years, to serve as a model for Taiwan's eventual reunification with the communist-ruled mainland.
Taiwan, which calls itself the Republic of China, is the vestige of the Nationalist government that ruled the mainland before 1949 when the communists won a long-drawn-out civil war.
In recent years Beijing and Taiwan have been sparring over what the mainland sees as provocative moves towards formal independence by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui.
Diplomats in Hong Kong said they expected Beijing-Taiwan talks in some shape or form to take place on the sidelines of the Hong Kong handover ceremonies.

International events have long proved tricky for the hosts when facing the issue of China versus Taiwan representation. China insists there must be no arrangements that imply recognition of "two Chinas".

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said in an interview with Hong Kong's flagship English language newspaper the South Cbina Morning Post on Monday that Hong Kong must serve as China's bridge to the world after July 1.
"China is going to continue economic development and reform, therefore we we still need Hong Kong as bridge and window."
He also signalled a hands-off approach to protests and press freedom in the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR, issues that the local government would be free to handle.

Qian said mainland bodies such as the Xinhua News Agency Hong Kong Branch, much reviled here for perceived meddling in handover politics and its watchdog role, and the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, would continue to exist.
But he said they would not "exercise leadership or interfere with the high degree of autonomy of the SAR".
Many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people have fretted that China might impsoe communist style repression.
But one of China's "red princelings", Hong Kong based entrepreneur Larry Yung was quoted in a Time magazine special as saying: If Hong Kong becomes a Chinese city, Hong Kong is dead."

Meanwhile a United Nations official reported progress in clearing out some of the remaining several thousand Vietnamese "boatpeople" held in Hong Kong since they fled communist ruled Vietnam. China has insisted they all be gone by July 1.
Preparations are gathering steam for Asia's "party of the century" in two weeks time. Hong Kong inaugurated a "media village" on Sunday to cope with a flood of 8,000 journalists.
Finishing touches were being laid to a new hospital for the Chinese People's Liberation Army garrison.
